title: HTML-first development and progressive enhancement
learningObjectives: Explain html-first development and progressive enhancement and the problem it addresses.
Use the relevant language or browser API with valid syntax.
Compare the technique with modern alternatives and identify when each is appropriate.
Handle errors, boundaries, security, and compatibility deliberately.
Test the implementation and explain its behaviour with evidence.

understand.concept: HTML-first development starts with meaningful, usable document content and native browser controls, then layers CSS and JavaScript enhancements on top. A form should have labels and a real action or a graceful fallback; links should navigate; buttons should perform a clearly defined action. JavaScript can improve validation, live search, transitions, or asynchronous updates, but the page should not become an empty shell when the script fails or loads late. Progressive enhancement is not a promise that every feature works without JavaScript; it is a design method that keeps essential content and core tasks robust.
understand.whyItMatters: HTML-first design improves resilience, accessibility, discoverability, and performance. It also makes the application easier to test because its basic behaviour exists before enhancement code is added.
understand.analogy: Build a working basic vehicle first, then add optional comfort and navigation features without removing the steering or brakes.
understand.analogyLimit: A web application may genuinely require JavaScript for its core purpose; progressive enhancement still means making loading, failure, and unsupported states explicit rather than pretending no script is needed.

explain.narrative: Create a search form that submits a query through a normal GET request. Add JavaScript to filter a local list instantly, but retain a useful non-script route or clear fallback.

examples.code: <form action="/search" method="get"><label for="q">Search lessons</label><input id="q" name="q" type="search"><button type="submit">Search</button></form>
examples.explanation: The form works through ordinary browser navigation when the server supports the endpoint. Labels and a submit button provide native semantics before JavaScript is added.
examples.expectedOutput: A labelled search field that submits a GET request to /search.

examples.explanation: The list content exists in HTML before the script runs. JavaScript adds an enhancement marker; if the script fails, the lesson list remains readable.
examples.expectedOutput: The three lessons remain visible; the data-enhanced attribute is added when JavaScript runs.

practise.guidedTask: Build a small search or contact page using semantic HTML first. Confirm its basic navigation and content work, then add a JavaScript enhancement without replacing the original structure.
practise.independentTask: Audit an existing page that renders all content from JavaScript. Refactor its essential content and navigation into HTML or a server-rendered response, then add enhancements with clear failure states.
hints: Start with meaningful HTML and native form controls.
Do not use a button for navigation or a link for an action.
Keep loading and script-failure states understandable.

questions.prompt: What is the first layer in HTML-first development?
options: Meaningful HTML content and native controls
questions.answer: Meaningful HTML content and native controls
questions.explanation: The document structure and core task should exist before optional enhancements.

options: Adding enhancements while preserving a useful core experience
Making every feature depend on animation
questions.answer: Adding enhancements while preserving a useful core experience
questions.explanation: Progressive enhancement layers capabilities onto a robust baseline.

questions.prompt: Which element should normally navigate to another URL?
questions.explanation: A link expresses navigation and provides native browser behaviour.

questions.prompt: Why are labels important in a basic form?
options: They programmatically identify controls and support usability
questions.answer: They programmatically identify controls and support usability
questions.explanation: Labels associate instructions with form controls and improve accessibility.

questions.prompt: Does progressive enhancement mean every web app must work fully without JavaScript?
options: No, essential functionality may require JS, but failure and fallback states should be deliberate
Yes, all JS must be removed
Only if the page contains images
questions.answer: No, essential functionality may require JS, but failure and fallback states should be deliberate
questions.explanation: The method aims for resilience and a useful baseline, not an unrealistic ban on JavaScript.
